title: Homemade instruments and the Hall brothers' first band
summary: Boys made reed instruments and a fishing-rod bass, the Hall brothers learned clarinet, and the band played dances up and down the river.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Well when you started off, did you have a real horn or did you make your own horn?

No, I had a. When we first started playing, we made some instruments, you know? Or a reed, canned reed, you know? And we made a bass with some fishing rod, you know? And we had a little club, you know? We made a club, me and Ed, Robert Hall, Ed, and all the brothers, you know? And different other fellas got together and things like that, you know? So finally, well, you know, well, their daddy was a clarinet player. Well they wanted to learn how to play clarinet. So what we did, we bought a clarinet, ten dollars. So Robert, yeah, Robert, he learned on the clarinet. Then Edmund learned on the clarinet. Then Hayward, or Calvin, he learned on the clarinet. Three of them. And the other one, the other one after one, he comes to the youngies. He's coming after and he's going to have to play. Herb, is he? Herb. Yeah, the one in New York. And the other one in the country where he picked up playing a bass on. He played in bands, the boys had a band out there, you know, a big band out there in the country, Susaphone. But well, I was playing around with them, you know what I mean? We couldn't play anymore, when we did start from the entrance, we couldn't play anymore about three songs, you know. We played all night, you know, three songs, playing slow this night, make time fast, you know what I mean? And the people liked it. So this man had a clubhouse, his wife followed. He was kicking on me. We couldn't play anymore than three songs. How many keys? We ain't no one key, that's all we know. You know what I mean? But we used to take one number at a time, you know what I mean? Until you get that, that's what you got to do with music, you know. So he played that, then after that, oh, we're beginning to get really good then. So the brother, he built a pavilion, really dance all day, you know. Oh well he was getting good then. Then after we started getting good, you know what we did, we brought a whole fellow out there who had a bar, well he's rich. We went to him and we sat down and explained to him what we had to do for us. He said yeah. So we stood for the influence for us. We got to make a room all, a whole set. It was a whole of them. It was a whole of them. We got to do the whole set and we played for this fellow. And the half time we started playing different places. Play on this side of the river, play on the other side of the river, you know what I mean? All of them down the river, you know what I mean? So, yeah. Did you like to work in the fields out there? No, I never did like to work. I never did like to work. I don't like to work. I never do work, you know what I mean, but I don't like it, you know what I mean? Oh yeah, I'll tell you the truth. I did a little bit of everything. I did a little bit of everything. I worked in a railroad shop. I worked on the railroad and rolled concrete. Sometimes building bridges and culverts, you know, tap all over culverts, put concrete, and once you start building bridges, you know, you know, you know, you know, you know, you can't stop, you see. You got to finish it because it's a setup, you see. Sometimes we'll be in the water up to here, to our neck. Well, yeah. I mean the cold water too, in the wintertime. And so, well, then I got this job in a railroad shop, right there. And after depression came, so I'm getting a little bit of a little bit of a little bit to build power
